# SK2191 — The struct is copied before the mutation lands

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A struct method that writes its own instance fields is called through an `in` parameter, a `ref readonly` local or a `foreach` variable, so the write goes to a copy and is discarded.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

A non-`readonly` member reached through a readonly-context receiver makes the compiler insert a defensive copy: the method runs, the fields change, and the object the caller is holding does not. Nothing throws, nothing warns, and the value read back afterwards is the one from before the call. ⚠ **AI-generated code produces this shape by default**, because a model writes `struct` without `readonly` and writes `in` on a parameter as a performance habit, and the two together are exactly the defect.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
struct Counter { public int Value; public void Increment() { Value++; } }

static void Bump(in Counter counter) => counter.Increment(); // writes a copy
```

Write:

```csharp
static Counter Bump(Counter counter) { counter.Increment(); return counter; }
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Disjoint from `SK2005` by receiver kind and not by a filter.** `SK2005` reports the same lost write through a `readonly` **field** and nothing else — its own `negative/parameter.cs` asserts silence on an `in` parameter. This rule takes the three receivers it does not have: an `in` or `ref readonly` parameter, a `ref readonly` local, and a `foreach` iteration variable. No receiver is both kinds, so neither rule can be configured into a duplicate of the other. ⚠ **The bar for "mutating" is a write the analysis has read, never the absence of a `readonly` modifier.** Almost nothing in real code marks struct members `readonly`, so reporting every non-`readonly` member reached through an `in` parameter would report most of a repository for a copy that is real and almost always harmless. The method must be non-static, void-returning, declared on a non-`readonly` struct **in the same file**, and its body must assign or increment an instance field at the top level — the identical evidence bar `SK2005` uses, shared in one place so the two cannot drift. Metadata bodies, other-file bodies, `[Conditional]` methods, expression trees, properties and indexers are excluded. ⚠ **The `foreach` case does not need a defensive copy to be the same bug**: the iteration variable is already a copy of the element, so the write is lost for a different mechanical reason and to exactly the same effect. `foreach (ref var item in span)` aliases the element and is excluded — the write lands, and that is what the `ref` is for. ⚠ **Nothing in the .NET analyzers covers this**, measured rather than assumed: a probe built outside this repository at `AnalysisMode=All` and `AnalysisLevel=latest-all` reports nothing on any of these shapes, and the compiler is silent too. Report-only: dropping `in`, taking the value by return, or marking the member `readonly` are three repairs that change three different things, and the call site does not say which was meant.
